description: Love, conditional acceptance, gender identity, financial wrongdoing, infidelity and the distance between generations.
content_html:
What the Play Asks Us to Believe

Things I Know to Be True draws its title from a phrase that challenges certainty. The things we know to be true about our families — their loyalty, their stability, their love — are exactly what the play systematically tests. Andrew Bovell structures the play's themes around the tension between what the Price family projects outwardly (a settled suburban life, parental pride, sibling solidarity) and what is actually concealed beneath that surface. For a dramatist, this gap between appearance and reality is a rich seam of dramatic irony.

Family: Conditional and Unconditional Love

The dominant theme of the play is family itself: what it can absorb, what it cannot, and who pays the cost of loyalty. Bovell explores two competing models of parental love through Bob and Fran. Fran's love is fierce and vocal; Bob's is quieter and harder to read. The play tests whether parental love is truly unconditional — offered regardless of what a child does or who they are — or whether it carries conditions that only a revelation can expose.

In staging this theme, a director working with the proxemics of the family group can communicate volumes before dialogue begins. When all six characters occupy the stage together, the distances between them — who stands near whom, who gravitates towards a parent, who is physically at the margin of the group — form an instant visual map of the family's emotional geography. A production using a proscenium arch configuration might arrange the family in a tableau that places Bob and Fran at the apex, with the four children arranged at varying distances, so that the staging enacts the theme of parental expectation as a gravitational force.

Key Fact

The central question of the play is whether the family's love is truly unconditional. Each of the four children's revelations tests this question from a different direction: departure, identity, criminality and grief.

Identity: Gender, Self-Determination and the Family's Gaze

The theme of identity runs through every character arc. For Mark, identity is the most explicit subject: the summer season stages the journey of a character coming forward with a truth about who they are in gender terms. Bovell handles this arc with dramatic care, showing the parents' different responses and the sibling dynamics around the revelation. For a performer, the challenge is to play the specific mixture of assertion and vulnerability that characterises a moment of authentic self-disclosure.

Frantic Assembly's movement sequences are structurally significant here. Contact improvisation and the round-by-through-under vocabulary can express the bodily dimension of identity — the sense of inhabiting a self more fully — in a way that pure dialogue cannot. A designer working on this section of the play might use cross-fading between lighting states to mark the transition between the family's before-and-after relationship with Mark / Mia, rather than a single sudden shift.

For Pip, identity is about self-determination: leaving a marriage and a city is an act of individual will that the family reads as abandonment. For Rosie, identity is the most existential: she is the character who must find meaning after heartbreak and who speaks from the play's narrative edge. Identity is also a theme for the parents themselves: Bob's late-revealed secret reframes who he is in the audience's understanding, retroactively altering the identity they believed they had witnessed across the whole play.

Examiners award marks for responses that treat this arc with specificity and respect for the character. Vague generalisations or language that editorialises about the subject matter earn no credit. Strong answers describe what a performer or director actually does on stage: specific vocal choices, specific physical choices, specific lighting and costume decisions that serve the character's journey at each stage of the arc.

A lighting designer might use a warm but precise lighting special on Mark / Mia during the revelation scene, isolating them from the family group while the family is lit in a broader, cooler wash. This separation in the lighting state communicates the character's position: fully present with the family yet briefly occupying a different emotional space. As Mia is accepted back into the family warmth, the isolated special can gradually fade into the shared wash, a visual enactment of inclusion.

Truth, Secrets and the Things We Don't Know

Alongside the children's revelations, the play harbours two parental secrets: Bob's concealed infidelity and the late-play shock that reframes his character. These secrets introduce the theme of truth itself as a complex, unstable thing. What the family has built together — their shared history, their mutual understanding — turns out to rest on partial information. Bovell suggests that all families are, to some degree, fictions that each member maintains for the others.

The rose garden carries this theme in physical form. A prop as symbol, the roses represent the beauty Bob cultivates and the concealment required to maintain it: a garden needs tending, work, constant management, just as a long marriage does. As a set designer, using the garden's seasonal change — spring blossom, summer fullness, autumn decay, bare winter stems — to mirror the play's structural arc makes the theme of concealed truth visible across the whole production.

Money, Ageing and Australian Suburbia

Ben's arc introduces the theme of financial wrongdoing and the gap between a child's projected success and their private reality. The theme here is the pressure of family expectation: the child who is supposed to have succeeded and has not. A performer playing Ben must communicate the layered quality of this shame — personal guilt, dread of a father's disappointment, awareness that his crime will affect the whole family.

Bovell also explores the theme of ageing parents and the moment when adult children see their parents as fallible. The Price parents are settled into late middle age when the play begins; by its end, they are irrevocably changed. The Australian suburban setting — a comfortable home, a tended garden, the domestic certainties of middle-class life in contemporary Adelaide — provides the context against which every destabilising revelation lands. The ordinariness of the setting is the point: the play insists that its themes are universal.

Students sometimes treat the play's themes as separate compartments — one child's arc = one theme. Bovell's work is more integrated than this. Identity runs through every character, not just Mark / Mia. Truth and concealment are as relevant to Bob's infidelity as to Ben's embezzlement. Family love is tested by Pip's departure just as much as by Ben's arrest. Strong exam answers draw thematic connections across the play rather than treating each season in isolation.

Key Fact

The rose garden embodies the play's central theme: the beauty that is cultivated outwardly and the concealment that sustains it. Designing the garden to change across the four seasons makes the theme of truth and hidden lives visible throughout the production.
exam_tip_html:
For the 12-mark question asking you to analyse playwright intentions on a moment related to theme, the most common error is describing what happens rather than explaining what Bovell wants the audience to feel or understand at that moment. Ask yourself: is Bovell testing the limits of unconditional love here? Is he staging the gap between private truth and public performance? What specific dramatic method (staging, structure, character interaction) is he using to make the theme visible, and what effect should that method have on the audience?

For the 20-mark staging response, if the question asks you to stage a key thematic moment, your answer must include both performer choices (vocal and physical) and at least one design discipline. For example, a question about the theme of identity and the Mark / Mia revelation demands: a specific lighting choice to stage the isolation and inclusion described above; a specific costume decision (what does Mia wear when she arrives, and how does that contrast with earlier scenes?); and specific performer choices for Fran and Bob (how does each parent physically respond to their child before they speak?).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The play's central theme is the tension between outward family stability and concealed individual truth: each revelation tests whether the Price family's love is conditional or unconditional.
  • Identity runs through every character arc, not just Mark / Mia's; the theme of truth and concealment connects Bob's infidelity, Ben's embezzlement and Pip's departure.
  • The rose garden is a prop-as-symbol that carries the theme of concealment across the whole production; a designer who changes the garden across the four seasons makes the play's thematic arc visible.

practice_questions.text: Name one theme of Things I Know to Be True related to family relationships.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: conditional/unconditional love; family secrets; parental expectation; the distance between generations; what holds a family together.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'dramatic irony'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic correct answer (e.g. when the audience knows something a character does not); 1 mark for development explaining how this creates tension or affects audience engagement (e.g. the audience's awareness of Bob's concealed secret makes every scene where he appears carry an additional layer of dramatic tension).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses the rose garden as a symbol to communicate the play's themes of concealment and truth.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the garden as a symbol (1); explanation of what it represents (Bob's emotional life, the work required to maintain appearances) (1); reference to the garden's seasonal change and how it mirrors the structural arc (1); a specific staging or design observation about how the symbol can be made visible (e.g. bare winter stems, a single cut rose as a prop) (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer could use changes in lighting state across the four seasons to communicate the play's themes of truth and concealment. Refer to specific lighting choices.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a specific seasonal lighting quality (e.g. warm amber wash for spring / summer; cool, stripped-back state for winter); 1 mark for explaining how the change in lighting state tracks the emotional arc of the play; 1 mark for a specific technical choice (e.g. a cross-fade between states, a suddenly harsher profile lantern for the revelation moment); 1 mark for explaining the effect of that choice on the audience's understanding of the themes.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses the play's structure and dramatic methods to explore the theme of conditional and unconditional parental love. Consider what the playwright intends the audience to question about the Price family by the end of the play.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis of Bovell's intentions across the seasonal structure, with specific reference to how different revelations test parental love in different ways. The student explains what Bovell wants the audience to question (whether any love is truly unconditional; whether the family's stability was ever real), with reference to dramatic methods (the withholding of Bob's secret, the direct-address passages that create dramatic irony, the Frantic Assembly movement sequences as moments of emotional truth). No plot summary.

Secure: Identifies the key revelations and their relation to parental love; makes some analytical comment about Bovell's intentions; references at least one dramatic method. Mostly analytical.

Developing: Describes what happens across the seasons without sustained analysis of Bovell's intentions or the effect on the audience.

Emerging: Retells the plot with little thematic analysis.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would stage the moment when the family reunites after a revelation that has tested their bonds. Using proxemics, lighting and costume, show how your staging communicates whether the family's love is conditional or unconditional. Refer to specific named choices and their effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A specific staging vision for a named reunion or confrontation moment. Proxemics: precise distances and angles for each character, with justification (e.g. Bob remains at an upstage distance but Fran crosses to her child downstage centre, the gap between the parents communicating their different responses); lighting: named state change or quality (e.g. a cross-fade into a warmer shared wash as acceptance is communicated); costume: specific choice for each character that signals their emotional position (e.g. a parent's everyday domestic costume contrasting with the returning child's travel-worn appearance). Every choice anchored to the named moment with audience effect explained.

Secure: Most disciplines addressed; at least one named lighting choice and clear proxemics thinking; audience effect generally stated; one area may be somewhat generic.

Developing: Relevant ideas; descriptive rather than analytical; limited technical specificity.

Emerging: Basic list of staging ideas without design specificity or thematic justification.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes the theme of 'conditional love' in the play?
options: Love that is freely given with no expectation of return
Love between two characters who are strangers
Love that is offered only when a person meets certain expectations
Love expressed only through physical contact

knowledge_checks.q: What does the rose garden symbolise in the play?
options: Bob's emotional life and the work required to maintain appearances
Fran's professional pride as a nurse

knowledge_checks.q: The emotional tension created when the audience has information that a character does not is called _____ .
An object or element of staging that carries meaning beyond its literal function is called a _____ .
Match each character to the theme their arc primarily explores:
right: Gender identity and the family's acceptance
Financial wrongdoing and the gap between projection and reality

flashcard_questions.q: What is the central thematic question of Things I Know to Be True?
flashcard_questions.a: Whether a family's love is truly unconditional.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the rose garden symbolise in the play?
flashcard_questions.a: Bob's emotional life and the work of concealment that sustains appearances.
When the audience has information that a character on stage does not.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the theme of identity encompass in the play?
What is a prop as symbol?
flashcard_questions.a: An object that carries meaning beyond its literal function in the staging.
The use of space and distance between performers to express relationship and status.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a cross-fade in lighting design?
flashcard_questions.a: A gradual transition between two lighting states.
A focused beam of light on a single performer or area.

flashcard_questions.q: What theme does Ben's embezzlement arc explore?
flashcard_questions.a: The gap between projected success and private reality under family expectation.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the setting of Australian suburban Adelaide contribute thematically?
flashcard_questions.a: It makes the play's themes universal: ordinary domesticity is the context for hidden crisis.

flashcard_questions.q: What Frantic Assembly movement technique expresses emotion the dialogue cannot carry?
flashcard_questions.a: Contact improvisation, such as chair duets.
The social, historical and cultural circumstances that shape a play and how audiences understand it.

glossary_terms.definition: The emotional tension created when the audience has information that one or more characters on stage do not.
The position and arrangement of performers relative to each other and to the audience, used to express status, relationship and emotional state.
An object, image or element of staging that carries significance beyond its literal function, representing an idea, relationship or emotional state.
A focused beam of light designed to illuminate a single performer or area of the stage.
The quality, colour and intensity of light on stage at a given moment.
Lighting using gradual transitions between states to suggest changing emotional atmosphere.
The social, historical and cultural circumstances that surround the creation of a play and that shape how audiences understand it.
